title: Stop Insider Trading Act
official_title: To amend chapter 131 of title 5 to require certain restrictions on stocks for Members of Congress and their spouses and dependents, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Steil (R-WI-1) with 93 cosponsors and cleared the House on July 22, 2026 before being received in the Senate. The House-passed version pairs Section 2 (stock-trading restrictions on Members of Congress and their spouses/dependent children, with referral-to-DOJ enforcement) with a Section 3 photo-identification requirement for federal elections that is not reflected in the bill's short title or CRS summary. The Senate would need 60 votes to invoke cloture on a general-order measure of this scope; the two-provision structure raises the difficulty of advancing the insider-trading provisions on their own without floor negotiation over Section 3.
summary: This bill has two operative sections. Section 2 bars Members of Congress and their spouses and dependent children from purchasing individual stocks, requires 7-to-14-day advance public notice before selling, and imposes a fee (greater of $2,000 or ten percent of transaction value, plus any net gain) for violations. Section 3 amends the Help America Vote Act to require in-person federal-election voters to present a state, federal, or Tribal photo identification, and mail voters to submit either a photo-ID copy, their last four Social Security digits with an affidavit, or a notarization.
brief: Bans stock purchases and requires advance sale notices for Members of Congress and their spouses/dependents, and separately requires photo ID for all federal-election voting.

top_lines.headline: Congressional Stock-Trading Ban
subs: Members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependent children may not purchase covered investments
Sales require public notice 7 to 14 calendar days before the sale, filed with the Clerk or Secretary and posted online
Covers securities of publicly traded companies and derivative equivalents like options and warrants

top_lines.headline: Exemptions from the Trading Ban
subs: Excepted investment funds (as described in section 13104(f)(8)) and comparable US-, state-, or territory-concentrated funds
Trusts where no covered individual has authority over the trustee, and the trustee is not a Member's spouse, child, parent, or sibling
Spouse or dependent trades made as part of a primary occupation or employer compensation, and automatic dividend reinvestments

top_lines.headline: Enforcement
subs: Fee equal to the greater of $2,000 or ten percent of the transaction value, plus any net gain realized
Fee cannot be paid from the Members' Representational Allowance, Senators' Official Personnel and Office Expense Account, or campaign contributions
Ethics office may refer former Members to DOJ if they resign or retire before paying

top_lines.headline: Federal Photo-ID Voting Requirement
subs: In-person federal-election voters must present a valid physical photo identification
Mail voters must submit a photo-ID copy, last four SSN digits with an inability affidavit, or notarization
Provisional ballot available if ID missing; ID or religious-photography-objection affidavit must be produced within 3 days

top_lines.headline: Accepted ID Types and State Duties
subs: State driver's license or ID card (with photo and expiration), U.S. passport, DoD or VA photo ID card, or Tribal-government ID with photo and expiration
States must provide free access to a digital imaging device (printer, copier, scanner) at courts, libraries, and police stations
States must notify voters of the ID requirement at registration and during online registration

items.main: Adds new Subchapter IV to chapter 131 of title 5, U.S. Code, prohibiting Members of Congress and their spouses and dependent children from purchasing individual securities of publicly traded companies or derivative equivalents.
items.detail: New section 13152(a) bars any "covered individual" from purchasing a covered investment, and section 13151 defines covered individuals as Members of Congress plus spouses and dependent children, and covered investments as publicly traded company securities or comparable synthetic interests (options, warrants, other derivatives). The prohibition takes effect 180 days after enactment.

items.main: Requires public advance notice 7 to 14 calendar days before any sale of a covered investment, filed with the Clerk of the House or Secretary of the Senate and posted online.
items.detail: New section 13152(b) requires each Member to file a notice of intent to sell — including projected sale date, description, and number of shares — for their own or a covered spouse or dependent's sale, no less than 7 and no more than 14 calendar days before the sale. The Clerk or Secretary must publish the notice and any withdrawal on a public website, and the notice must be withdrawn if the sale is called off.

items.main: Sets enforcement through a fee equal to the greater of $2,000 or ten percent of the transaction value, plus any net gain realized during the coverage period, and imposes divestiture for illegal purchases.
items.detail: New section 13153 directs the supervising ethics office to impose the fee on the Member who caused the violation (or whose spouse or child did) and to require the sale of any covered investment purchased in violation of section 13152(a). Members may not pay the fee from the Members' Representational Allowance, Senators' Official Personnel and Office Expense Account, campaign contributions (as defined in section 301(8) of the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971), or other Federal-office donations. Fees are deposited to the Treasury general fund as miscellaneous receipts. The ethics office may refer a former Member who resigns or retires before paying to the Department of Justice, with section 13106 applied the same as for a direct violation.

sections.label: Section 3 — Photo Identification Requirements for Federal Elections

items.main: Adds a new section 303A to the Help America Vote Act of 2002 (52 U.S.C. 21081 et seq.) requiring in-person voters in federal elections to present a valid physical photo identification.
items.detail: State or local election officials may not provide an in-person federal-election ballot without a valid physical photo ID. A voter without ID may cast a provisional ballot but the eligibility determination under HAVA section 302(a)(4) may not be made unless, within 3 days, the voter presents the required ID or an affidavit — developed and made available by the State — attesting to a religious objection to being photographed.

items.main: Requires mail and other non-in-person voters to submit a photo-ID copy, the last four digits of their Social Security number plus an inability affidavit, or a notarization by a notary public.
items.detail: New section 303A(a)(2) blocks acceptance of non-in-person ballots unless the voter submits (i) a copy of a valid photo identification, (ii) the last four SSN digits and a state-provided affidavit attesting to inability to obtain a copy after reasonable efforts, or (iii) a notary-attested statement that the voter personally marked the ballot. Exempted are absent uniformed services voters as defined in section 107(1) of the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act (52 U.S.C. 20310(1)) and individuals voting under section 3(b)(2)(B)(ii) of the Voting Accessibility for the Elderly and Handicapped Act.

items.main: Defines the accepted forms of valid photo identification and imposes new state duties to publicize the requirement and to provide free public access to copying equipment.
items.detail: Accepted IDs are: a State-issued driver's license or motor-vehicle-authority ID card (each with photo and expiration date), a valid U.S. passport, a DoD or VA photo ID card, or a photo ID document with expiration date issued by a Tribal government. States must ensure, to the extent practicable, free public access to a digital imaging device (printer, copier, image scanner, or multifunction machine) at state and local government buildings including courts, libraries, and police stations, for making photo-ID copies. States must notify individuals of the photo-ID requirement at the time of voter registration, including before completion of online registration. Section 3 takes effect 90 days after enactment.

underreported.summary: The bill inserts a new HAVA section 303A imposing a federal photo-ID requirement on all in-person voting and a photo-ID or SSN-plus-affidavit requirement on all non-in-person voting in federal elections.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's short title is the "Stop Insider Trading Act" and the CRS summary describes only the stock-trading restrictions on Members of Congress. The photo-ID rule is a stand-alone federal election-administration mandate on all states, mechanically unrelated to the insider-trading subject in the title.

underreported.summary: Section 401 of HAVA (52 U.S.C. 21111) is amended so its scope reference reads "subtitle A of title III" instead of "sections 301, 302, 303, and 304."
underreported.why_unreported: The section is labeled "Conforming Amendment Relating to Enforcement," but the change replaces the four enumerated section references with a subtitle-wide reference — a scope-of-reference change that the short label does not signal.

underreported.summary: The stock-purchase ban applies to a Member's spouse and dependent children as well as the Member.
underreported.why_unreported: The public-facing framing focuses on Members' own trading; the operative rule reaches household-member portfolios, subject to the occupational and dividend-reinvestment exceptions in section 13152(c).

underreported.summary: The enforcement fee includes not just $2,000 or ten percent but also any net gain realized on the covered investment from the date the individual became a covered individual through disposition.
underreported.why_unreported: The headline penalty is "$2,000 or ten percent," but the second, uncapped component can vastly exceed the flat or percentage fee for a long-held position that appreciated during a covered individual's tenure.

gaps: The bill bans covered individuals from purchasing new covered investments but does not require Members already holding covered investments on the effective date to divest, nor set any deadline for disposing of pre-existing holdings.

The bill's insider-trading restrictions apply only to Members of Congress, spouses, and dependent children — the bill does not address covered financial holdings of Executive Branch officials, federal judges, or Congressional staff.

Section 3 requires a valid photo identification for federal-election voting but does not appropriate any funds to help states issue free voter-eligible ID cards or to operate the required copying devices at courts, libraries, and police stations.

Section 3 provides a religious-photography-objection affidavit path but no equivalent affidavit path for voters who lack photo identification for non-religious reasons (e.g. lost, stolen, expired, or unaffordable ID) at in-person voting.

The bill's enforcement mechanism for the insider-trading section is a fee plus divestiture — the bill does not create a criminal penalty for a Member who trades on non-public information, leaving that conduct to existing securities law.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Perry
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, I am a proud original cosponsor of not only this bill but every other bipartisan bill that is not here. The record for me is clear on this. Last year alone, Members made, according to my count, over 13,000 trades, totaling over $600 million with 202 representatives and 56 senators trading, both Republican and Democrat. Every single year, at some point, somebody publishes a list of the Members that were most successful in trading.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Miller
featured_quotes.text: As Members of the United States Congress, it is our job to preserve the integrity of this institution and take seriously the responsibility placed on us by our constituents. This legislation will bring about a more transparent and accountable Congress and will be a strong measure to restore the American people's trust in this institution. While older laws have prohibited Members from using nonpublic information when trading, they did not go far enough. More robust measures should be put in place, and that is exactly what this bill does.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Krishnamoorthi
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, I have helped lead bipartisan efforts to ban stock trading by Members of Congress, and I am deeply frustrated that the majority refuses to take the issue seriously enough at this crucial time when Congress' stock is at an all-time low. We should not be playing partisan games on this. The Republican majority is pushing a bill that still allows Members of Congress to hold, sell, and even buy certain individual stocks.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Lawler
featured_quotes.text: It must be the everyday expectation of every American. For too long, the public has watched the headlines that read like a civic lesson gone wrong: elected officials buying and selling stocks in industries they regulate, profiting from information the public will never see. That is not merely unseemly, it is corrosive. It eats away at confidence in this institution, and confidence once lost is not easily rebuilt. Banning congressional stock trading is a simple proposition. If someone serves the public, they serve only the public.

added: New Subchapter IV of chapter 131 of title 5, U.S. Code (new sections 13151, 13152, 13153) — stock-trading restrictions on Members of Congress and covered household members
New section 303A of the Help America Vote Act — federal-election photo identification requirement for in-person and non-in-person voting
modified: Table of contents for chapter 131 of title 5, U.S. Code — new Subchapter IV entries added
HAVA section 311(b) (52 U.S.C. 21101(b)) — new paragraph (4) directing Election Assistance Commission voluntary guidance on section 303A within 90 days of enactment
HAVA section 401 (52 U.S.C. 21111) — enforcement scope changed from "sections 301, 302, 303, and 304" to "subtitle A of title III"
